transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-09-29 14:30 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Lena (Hearthwell), Omar (Hearthwell), Priya (Hearthwell)

Summary: Quick scoping to decide network approach for the POC and to size benchmark runs. Customer cares about data not leaving EU region, egress policing, and minimizing cross-VPC traffic while keeping latency under tight SLAs.

00:00 Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick goal for today is to pick a network pattern and agree benchmark targets and a pilot timeline.
00:27 Lena (Head ML): Yep, main ask from compliance is that any PHI-ish vectors stay in eu-west-1, we need proof that inference traffic stays within region unless explicitly allowed.
00:40 Carlos (SE): Understood. There are two common patterns we recommend: VPC peering, which is more straightforward but can be harder to audit at scale, and AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) which gives per-service egress control. Either works with Redwood Private but tradeoffs on throughput and NATing.
01:05 Omar (Cloud): Quick Q — if we do peering, do we have to route all egress through our NAT? We want to avoid unexpected egress to public internet.
01:18 Carlos: You can lock egress at the subnet/NACL level; for peering traffic to Redwood's endpoints you'd point to the peered route. Note that peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs. Also quick note, our dedicated zones expect TLS to Redwood endpoints; we support cert pinned connections and customer KMS for keys.
01:35 Priya (Security): Are audit logs pushed to our S3 in-region or do they land in Redwood's bucket?
01:44 Maya: Default is logs to Redwood's control plane but for Private deployments we can push audit logs to a customer-owned S3 or support log forwarding. We'll send the SOC2 and logging design doc.
02:05 Lena: We also have egress constraints for third-party telemetry — things like Datadog and Sentry are allowed but must be explicit.
02:18 Carlos: Noted, in the pilot we can set an allowlist for specific hostnames and IPs. We'll provide a sample ip/host allowlist and a policy template.
03:00 Maya: Benchmarks — what are your targets? We asked earlier for typical request size and concurrency but wanted to confirm in call.
03:12 Lena: Typical inference call for us is 200–600 tokens, average 350. Concurrency varies but we need sustained throughput of 120 req/s at peak and p99 under 250ms if possible.
03:30 Carlos: That p99 250ms is tight if you have long sequences; we typically recommend aiming for p50 < 80ms and p95 <150ms for gen models with batching tuned. We'll design a microbenchmark and a realistic conversational workload. For throughput we'll run multi-client load to simulate spikes.
04:05 Omar: For region locking, we need the entire inference path to stay in eu-west-1, does Redwood Dedicated support region pinned nodes?
04:17 Maya: Yes, Redwood Dedicated / Private supports region pinning. For hosted models we can provision dedicated capacity in eu-west-1. For Private we can deploy a control plane limited to your VPC; there are some firewall and routing steps.
04:40 Priya: PrivateLink was mentioned earlier — which do you recommend for compliance?
04:50 Carlos: PrivateLink gives you interface endpoints and is easier to show in the network diagrams for auditors because traffic never traverses the public internet. Peering is fine but you need to show controls for route propagation and NATs. For high throughput, peering may give simpler throughput characteristics; PrivateLink can be burst-limited by ENIs but usually fine for POC sizes.
05:20 Lena: Are there cost differences we should expect?
05:27 Maya: Yes, PrivateLink has per-GB and per-hour costs for endpoints; peering is usually free within account but you might pay for data transfer in cross-account peering depending on cloud provider policies. We will include cost scenarios in the doc.
06:00 Carlos: About benchmarks — we'll propose three phases: baseline single-VM latency tests, scaled throughput tests across multiple clients, and long-run stability with realistic prompts. We'll use your sample prompts and Redwood's micro-bench harness.
06:24 Omar: For the harness, can we run it from within our VPC to hit the interface endpoint?
06:30 Carlos: Yes, we'll provide a script and a Docker image you can run in your subnets. The harness will emit detailed token-level timing and kv-cache stats (note: transcription earlier trips up KV cache as K-V cash in some docs).
07:05 Priya: On keys — can we use our KMS for model request encryption or do you require Redwood-managed KMS?
07:16 Maya: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM for encryption at rest and envelope encryption. For hosted endpoints, we can use customer-managed keys in cross-account setup — we'll include the KMS diagram.
08:00 Lena: Success criteria for the pilot: 1) demonstrate p99 latency below 300ms for 90% of realistic traffic, 2) prove egress logging and allowlisting works with our SIEM, 3) show that data never routes outside eu-west-1 for flagged payloads.
08:35 Carlos: We'll propose a scoring matrix and concrete test cases to validate each criteria.
09:00 Omar: Timeline — how long to set up networking and bench?
09:10 Maya: Typical POC timeline is 3 weeks: week 1 network & access + test infra, week 2 run microbenchmarks and iterate on config, week 3 stability tests and wrap up.
09:30 Lena: That works; procurement needs a one-page SOW.
09:35 Maya: We'll prepare a short SOW and pilot agreement after this call.
10:00 Carlos: Technical note — if you plan to pin model versions, we need to know the model family (llama-2- style or MPT) and max sequence lengths; that affects kernel choices and latency.
10:24 Lena: Most of our production usage is an ensemble of a smaller instruct model and a reranker. Average sequence length 512 tokens for some rerankers.
10:40 Carlos: Great, we'll include quantization/throughput recommendations. For 512 seqs we'll probably recommend 16GB GPUs for latency runs and 80–100GB pooled capacity for throughput depending on QPS.
11:10 Omar: Any blockers for peering vs PrivateLink from Redwood side?
11:18 Maya: No blockers, just config steps. For PrivateLink we need to create interface endpoints in your account and you need to accept the endpoint connections. For peering you'll provide the CIDR and we’ll propose a routeset. We'll share exact Security Group templates.
12:00 Priya: About logs — we need all request/response metadata stripped for storage then forwarded to our SIEM. Is redaction suported? (sic)
12:12 Carlos: We have redaction hooks in the pipeline; for Private deployments we can deploy the redaction lambda in your account so raw payloads never leave. We'll document how to configure it.
13:00 Maya: I'll also share our security attestations (SOC2, ISO) and the deployment checklist.
13:25 Lena: For benchmarks, one more ask: can you run a cross-availability-zone test to show p95/p99 impact?
13:33 Carlos: Yes, we'll include an AZ-cross test to quantify intra-region AZ networking variance.
14:00 Maya: Recap and next steps — we will: 1) share SOW + network template, 2) share benchmark harness and sample payloads (link: drive/bench/harness), 3) customer to share CIDRs and data residency list, 4) schedule pilot kickoff.
14:28 Omar: We'll get CIDRs and schedule a procurement sync.
14:35 Priya: We'll review the SOW with legal and circle back.

Action items (in-meeting):
- Maya: upload SOW and network template link to shared drive
